passage: The video ended at one in the morning, and Nandini was wide awake. A self-taught founder, no college, a company by twenty. “Why waste years on Class 11 and 12?” she told her cousin Yogesh the next day. “I'll learn everything myself.” Yogesh said, “Didn't he say his savings covered two years, an uncle gave him a room, and he'd been coding since he was twelve?” “That's just background.” She stopped preparing for the pre-boards and spent evenings watching more founder interviews. By March she had a notebook of app ideas, no working app, and a maths score that slid from seventy-two to fifty-five. Yogesh watched her scroll through another interview and said nothing this time.

"I'm not going to college," Aadhya announced at dinner. "I watched this video about a founder who dropped out and built a company worth crores. He taught himself everything."

Her cousin Jeevan, visiting for the week, put down his roti. "Did the video say where he got his first money?"

"He just... started."

"Look again." Jeevan pulled up the video on his phone and scrubbed ahead. "His parents gave him savings. He'd been coding for six years before he dropped out. And his uncle introduced him to his first investors."

Aadhya frowned. "Well, I can learn fast too."

"You've been learning design for two months. And you don't have an uncle with investors."

Aadhya went quiet. She had already told her friends she was skipping college applications. Two deadlines had passed that week.

qa.q: How long had Aadhya been learning design?
How did Aadhya feel when Jeevan listed the founder's advantages?
qa.a: She felt deflated and defensive, going quiet after insisting she could learn fast too.

qa.q: What would have been a wiser way to use the founder's story?
qa.a: Taking what's useful, like practising skills every day, while still applying to college, since the founder had savings, contacts and years of practice she lacks.

qa.q: How might Aadhya's parents see her announcement?
qa.a: They might feel alarmed and worried, especially about the missed application deadlines.

grounding: Shows a teen deciding to skip formal study after a video about a self-taught founder, overlooking the founder's savings, contacts and years of practice.

subtype: Approach: copying a famous role model's path [Pitfall]
passage:
At fifteen, I watched a video that changed my plans, for about three months. I'm Gopika, and the video was about a woman who skipped university, taught herself fashion design and now runs a clothing label. It was beautifully edited. I watched it maybe thirty times.

I told my parents I wouldn't take the science stream or any stream that led to college. I'd learn design from videos and start a label.

My friend Wasim asked a simple question: "How did she pay for her first collection?" I looked it up. Her family owned a textile business. She'd sewn since she was ten. She had a mentor in the industry.

I had a secondhand sewing machine and three months of tutorials.

I felt stupid for a while. But I also felt relieved. I chose humanities with a design elective and kept sewing on weekends. The dream stayed. The shortcut didn't.

qa.q: How many times did Gopika watch the video?
How did Gopika feel after learning about the designer's background?
qa.a: Gopika felt stupid for a while but also relieved.

qa.q: What else could Gopika do to keep building towards the dream?
qa.a: Gopika could look for a local tailor or designer to learn from, since the founder's mentor was a big part of her story.

qa.q: How might Wasim see Gopika's final choice?
qa.a: Wasim probably feels glad the question helped, seeing Gopika keep the dream while choosing a steadier route.

grounding: A reflective account of a teen who nearly skipped formal study after a video about a self-taught founder, overlooking the founder's savings, contacts and years of practice.
